name: hearth

attributes.attribute: central spiritual symbol of the home connected with the Otherworld
site of the cooking fire and of sacrifices to the family's ancestors
liminal space that drew fairies and ghosts
on Samhain the ghosts of the dead appeared by the fire

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The hearth was a significant spiritual symbol for the Celts. It stood at the center of the home, and the Celts connected that center with the Otherworld. The cooking fire blazed there and in most cases heated the home as well. Early archaeological sites show an emphasis on the hearth. It was decorated with divine symbols, like the ram's-head andirons found in Gaul. People believed sacrifices to the family's ancestors took place at each home's hearth. The hearth was a liminal space, not wholly of this world but opening out to the world of spirits. Fairies and ghosts gathered there, most keenly on pivotal days. On Samhain, the beginning of winter on November 1, the ghosts of the dead sometimes appeared by the fire. They sat or warmed themselves in a familiar place, calmly smoking or knitting.

okr.objective: Document the hearth as the Celtic sacred center of the home.
key_results: Record the hearth as the symbol of the home's center tied to the Otherworld.
Describe the ancestor sacrifices and the liminal nature of the place.
Note the Samhain ghost gathering and the ram's-head andirons of Gaul.
